<skill>
<name>wayfinder</name>
<path>/home/kafka/.agents/skills/wayfinder/SKILL.md</path>
---
name: wayfinder
description: Plan a huge chunk of work — more than one agent session can hold — as a shared map of decision tickets on your issue tracker, and resolve them one at a time until the way to the destination is clear.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

A loose idea has arrived — too big for one agent session, and wrapped in fog: the way from here to the **destination** isn't visible yet. Wayfinding is about finding that way, not charging at the destination. This skill charts the way as a **shared map** on the repo's issue tracker, then works its **decision tickets** — questions whose resolution is a decision, not slices of a build to execute — one at a time until the route is clear.

The destination varies per effort, and naming it is the first act of charting — it shapes every ticket. It might be a spec to hand off and iterate on, a decision to lock before planning starts, or a change made in place like a data-structure migration. The map is domain-agnostic — engineering work, course content, whatever fits the shape.

## Plan, don't do

Wayfinder is **planning** by default: each ticket resolves a decision, and the map is done when the way is clear — nothing left to decide before someone goes and does the thing. The pull to just do the work is usually the signal you've reached the edge of the map and it's time to hand off. An effort can override this in its **Notes** — carrying execution into the map itself — but absent that, produce decisions, not deliverables.

## Refer by name

Every map and ticket is an issue, so it has a **name** — its title. In everything the human reads — narration, the map's Decisions-so-far — refer to it by that name, never by a bare id, number, or slug. A wall of `#42, #43, #44` is illegible; names read at a glance. The id and URL don't vanish — a name wraps its link — but they ride *inside* the name, never stand in for it.

## The Map

The map is a single issue on this repo's issue tracker, labelled `wayfinder:map` — the canonical artifact. Its tickets are child issues of the map.

The map is an **index**, not a store. It lists the decisions made and points at the tickets that hold their detail; a decision lives in exactly one place — its ticket — so the map never restates it, only gists it and links.

**Where the map, its child tickets, blocking, and frontier queries physically live is tracker-specific.** The issue tracker should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not. Consult the tracker doc's "Wayfinding operations" section for how _this_ repo expresses them. If no tracker has been provided, default to the local-markdown tracker.

### The map body

The whole map at low resolution, loaded once per session. Open tickets are **not** listed — they are open child issues, found by query.

```markdown
## Destination

<what reaching the end of this map looks like — the spec, decision, or change this effort is finding its way to. One or two lines; every session orients to it before choosing a ticket.>

## Notes

<domain; skills every session should consult; standing preferences for this effort>

## Decisions so far

<!-- the index — one line per closed ticket: enough to judge relevance, then zoom the link for the detail the ticket holds -->

- [<closed ticket title>](link) — <one-line gist of the answer>

## Not yet specified

<!-- see "Fog of war": in-scope fog you can't ticket yet; graduates as the frontier advances -->

## Out of scope

<!-- see "Out of scope": work ruled beyond the destination; closed, never graduates -->
```

### Tickets

Each ticket is a **child issue** of the map; the tracker's issue id is its identity. Its body is the question, sized to one 100K token agent session:

```markdown
## Question

<the decision or investigation this ticket resolves>
```

Each ticket carries a `wayfinder:<type>` label — one of `research`, `prototype`, `grilling`, `task` (see [Ticket Types](#ticket-types)).

A session **claims** a ticket by assigning it to the dev driving the map, **first**, before any work, so concurrent sessions skip it. That assignee _is_ the claim: an open, unassigned ticket is unclaimed.

Blocking uses the tracker's **native** dependency relationship — essential because it renders the frontier _visually_ in the tracker's own UI, so the human sees what's takeable without opening the map. Only a tracker that lacks native blocking falls back to a body convention. A ticket is **unblocked** when every ticket blocking it is closed; the **frontier** is the open, unblocked, unclaimed children — the edge of the known.

The answer isn't part of the body — it's recorded on resolution (see [Work through the map](#work-through-the-map)). Assets created while resolving a ticket are linked from the issue, not pasted in.

## Ticket Types

Every ticket is either **HITL** — human in the loop, worked *with* a human who speaks for themselves — or **AFK**, driven by the agent alone. A HITL ticket only resolves through that live exchange; the agent never stands in for the human's side of it (a grilling agent that answers its own questions has broken this).

- **Research** (AFK): Reading documentation, third-party APIs, or local resources like knowledge bases to surface a fact a decision waits on. Resolved by a `/research` **subagent**. Use when knowledge outside the current working directory is required.
- **Prototype** (HITL): Raise the fidelity of the discussion by making a cheap, rough, concrete artifact to react to — an outline, a rough take, a stub, or UI/logic code via the /prototype skill. Links the prototype as an asset. Use when "how should it look" or "how should it behave" is the key question.
- **Grilling** (HITL): Conversation via the /grilling and /domain-modeling skills, one question at a time. The default case.
- **Task** (HITL or AFK): Manual work that must happen before a *decision* can be made — nothing to decide, prototype, or research, but the discussion is blocked until it's done. Signing up for a service so its API can be judged, provisioning access, moving data so its shape can be seen. This is the one type that *does* rather than decides — and it earns its place by unblocking a decision, not by delivering the destination. The agent drives it alone where it can (AFK); otherwise it hands the human a precise checklist (HITL). Resolved when the work is done; the answer records what was done and any resulting facts (credentials location, new URLs, row counts) later tickets depend on.

## Fog of war

The map is _deliberately_ incomplete: don't chart what you can't yet see. Beyond the live tickets lies the **fog of war** — the dim view of decisions and investigations you can tell are coming but can't yet pin down, because they hang on questions still open. Resolving a ticket clears the fog ahead of it, graduating whatever's now specifiable into fresh tickets — one at a time, until the way to the destination is clear and no tickets remain.

The map's **Not yet specified** section is where that dim view is written down: the suspected question, the area to revisit later. It's the undiscovered frontier _toward_ the destination — everything here is in scope, just not sharp enough to ticket. Write as loosely or as fully as the view allows; it doubles as a signpost for collaborators reading where the effort is headed.

**Fog or ticket?** The test is whether you can state the question precisely now — _not_ whether you can answer it now.

- **Ticket when** the question is already sharp — even if it's blocked and you can't act on it yet.
- **Not yet specified when** you can't yet phrase it that sharply. Don't pre-slice the fog into ticket-sized pieces: it's coarser than a ticket, and one patch may graduate into several tickets, or none, once the frontier reaches it.

**Not yet specified** excludes what's already decided (Decisions so far), what's already a live ticket, and what's out of scope (the next section).

## Out of scope

Fog only ever gathers _toward_ the destination. The destination fixes the scope, so work beyond it is **out of scope** — it isn't fog, and it doesn't belong in **Not yet specified**. It gets its own **Out of scope** section on the map: work you've consciously ruled out of _this_ effort. Scope, not sharpness, lands it here.

Out-of-scope work never graduates — the frontier stops at the destination — so it returns only if the destination is redrawn, and then as a fresh effort, not a resumption.

Ruling something out of scope is a scoping act, not a step on the route. When a ticket that already exists turns out to sit past the destination — mis-scoped in while charting, or exposed by a resolution — **close it** (a closed ticket is unambiguously off the frontier) and leave one line in the **Out of scope** section: the gist plus why it's out of scope, linking the closed ticket. It stays out of **Decisions so far**, which records the route actually walked — a scope boundary isn't a step on it.

## Invocation

Two modes. Either way, **never resolve more than one ticket per session** — with the exception of research tickets.

### Chart the map

User invokes with a loose idea.

1. **Name the destination.** Run a `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` session to pin down what this map is finding its way to — the spec, decision, or change. The destination fixes the scope, so it's settled first.
2. **Map the frontier.** Grill again, **breadth-first** this time: fan out across the whole space rather than deep on any one thread, surfacing the open decisions and the first steps takeable now. **If this surfaces no fog** — the way to the destination is already clear, the whole journey small enough for one session — you don't need a map. Stop and ask the user how they'd like to proceed.
3. **Create the map** (label `wayfinder:map`): Destination and Notes filled in, Decisions-so-far empty, the fog sketched into **Not yet specified**.
4. **Create the tickets you can specify now** as child issues of the map — then wire blocking edges in a **second pass** (issues need ids before they can reference each other). Wiring sorts them into the frontier and the blocked; everything you can't yet specify stays in the fog — the **Not yet specified** section.
5. **Fire the research subagents.** For each `research` ticket you just created, spin up a `/research` subagent to resolve it in parallel, capturing its findings on a throwaway `research/<name>` branch with a context pointer from the ticket.
6. Stop — charting is one session's work; it hand-resolves nothing.

### Work through the map

User invokes with a map (URL or number). A ticket is **optional** — without one, you pick the next decision, not the user.

1. Load the **map** — the low-res view, not every ticket body.
2. Choose the ticket. If the user named one, use it. Otherwise take the first frontier ticket in order. **Claim it**: assign it to yourself before any work.
3. Resolve it — **zoom as needed**: fetch the full body of any related or closed ticket on demand; invoke the skills the `## Notes` block names. If in doubt, use `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling`.
4. Record the resolution: post the answer as a **resolution comment**, **close** the issue, and **append a context pointer** to the map's Decisions-so-far.
5. Add newly-surfaced tickets (create-then-wire); graduate any fog the answer has made specifiable, clearing each graduated patch from **Not yet specified** so it lives only as its new ticket. If the answer reveals a ticket — this one or another — sits beyond the destination, **rule it out of scope** rather than resolving it on the route. If the decision invalidates other parts of the map, update or delete those tickets.

The user may run unblocked tickets in parallel, so expect other sessions to be editing the tracker concurrently.

</skill>

content.text:
“Define the minimal sighting persistence contract” is claimed and ready for our grilling session.

First decision: how should a sighting be identified?

I recommend a server-generated `bigint` identity primary key. It is the smallest adequate contract for this private, single-person app: the durable save returns the ID, correction updates that row, and deletion targets it. UUIDs add complexity without a current need for offline creation, distributed writers, or public unguessable URLs.

Duplicate label dates and times should still be allowed—the ID identifies the observation, while label time is recorded data rather than identity.

Do you agree with a server-generated `bigint` identity, or do you want UUID-based identifiers?
How big is bigint compared to next step down

In PostgreSQL:

- `bigint`: 8 bytes, up to about 9.2 quintillion positive IDs.
- `integer`: 4 bytes, up to about 2.1 billion positive IDs.

For this single-person tracker, `integer GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY` is more than enough. At 100 sightings every day, exhaustion would take roughly 58,000 years. It also avoids JavaScript’s `bigint`/JSON serialization friction.

I revise my recommendation to a server-generated 4-byte `integer` identity. Do you agree?
Yeah

Identity is settled: each sighting gets a server-generated PostgreSQL `integer` identity; duplicate label times remain valid.

Next decision: how should the timezone-free label date and minute be stored?

I recommend two columns:

- `label_date date`
- `label_minute smallint`, constrained to `0–1439` minutes after midnight

This exactly represents the established domain meaning, makes seconds and timezone conversion impossible, and keeps planner window and 15-minute-bucket arithmetic straightforward. The application can translate `870` to `2:30 PM` at its boundary.

The alternative is one `timestamp without time zone`, which looks more familiar but invites developers and libraries to mistake it for an instant.

Do you agree with `label_date` plus `label_minute`?
Any reason we can’t just store as a varchar (7) for XX:XXam / XX:XXpm then parse?

We could, but it would turn presentation text into the canonical data format.

Problems with `varchar(7)` include:

- Lexical ordering is not chronological: `12:00pm` sorts before `2:00pm`.
- Every planner query must parse the string before doing ±10-minute comparisons.
- Weekday/time aggregation and 15-minute bucketing become more cumbersome.
- Variations such as `2:05pm`, `02:05PM`, and whitespace require strict validation.
- Changing the UI to 24-hour time or localized formatting would require parsing stored display text.
- PostgreSQL cannot naturally enforce that the value is a real clock time without a complex constraint.

Storage savings would also be negligible: a seven-character `varchar` value needs roughly eight bytes including its length header, while a `smallint` needs two.

I still recommend storing `label_minute` as `0–1439` and formatting it as `h:mm AM/PM` only for display. Does that settle the representation?
I guess it makes doing data analysis queries harder too huh

Exactly. With an integer minute, analysis is direct:

- Hour: `label_minute / 60`
- 15-minute bucket: `label_minute / 15`
- ±10-minute window: numeric range comparison
- Chronological sorting: ordinary numeric ordering
- Morning/afternoon filtering: compare against `720`

With a string, every query must first parse AM/PM text into a numeric time, creating more complexity and more opportunities for malformed data.

Shall we lock in `label_date date` plus `label_minute smallint`?
Yeah

Locked in: label time is stored as `label_date date` plus `label_minute smallint` constrained to `0–1439`.

Next decision: doneness representation.

I recommend nullable text constrained to exactly `light`, `medium`, or `dark`. This preserves the domain language directly, avoids a hidden numeric mapping such as `1 = light`, and is easier to evolve than a PostgreSQL enum. `NULL` means doneness was not recorded.

Do you agree with constrained nullable text?
I’m not familiar with constrained text. Is it exactly what it sounds like

Yes. The column stores ordinary text, while a database `CHECK` constraint rejects anything outside the allowed values.

Conceptually:

```sql
doneness text
  CHECK (doneness IN ('light', 'medium', 'dark'))
```

Because the column is nullable, these are valid:

```text
NULL
light
medium
dark
```

Values such as `well-done`, `Medium`, or an empty string are rejected by PostgreSQL.

It gives us readable data without creating a dedicated PostgreSQL enum type. Shall we use it?
Interesting yeah

Locked in: `doneness` is nullable constrained text with `light`, `medium`, and `dark` as its only non-null values.

Next: audit timestamps.

I recommend two server-generated `timestamptz` columns:

- `created_at`: when the sighting was first saved; immutable
- `updated_at`: initially the same time, advanced whenever label time or doneness changes

These are real system events, so unlike label time they should represent instants with timezone-aware timestamps. Recent Sightings should sort by `created_at`, ensuring a newly recorded backfill still appears first; editing should not move an old sighting to the top.

Do you agree with both timestamps and that ordering behavior?
Yeah

Locked in: immutable `created_at`, mutable `updated_at`, both timezone-aware; Recent Sightings orders by creation time rather than label time or edit time.

Next: mutation shape.

I recommend:

- Create accepts required `labelDate` and `labelMinute`, plus optional `doneness`, then returns the complete persisted sighting.
- Update replaces all three editable fields together: `labelDate`, `labelMinute`, and nullable `doneness`, then returns the complete updated sighting.
- The save-then-enrich flow uses that same update operation after creation.
- No optimistic-lock version is needed for one user and one expected writer.

A full replacement update is slightly less terse than arbitrary patches, but it avoids ambiguity between “doneness omitted” and “clear doneness to `NULL`.”

Do you agree with create plus full-replacement update?
What are nuances around full replace vs spot patches

A full replacement sends the complete editable state:

```ts
{
  labelDate: "2026-08-01",
  labelMinute: 870,
  doneness: "medium",
}
```

A spot patch sends only changes:

```ts
{ doneness: "medium" }
```

Full replacement advantages:

- One unambiguous validation path.
- Omitted fields cannot accidentally mean “leave unchanged.”
- Clearing doneness is simply `doneness: null`.
- The returned form state can be treated as the whole saved record.

Its main risk is stale overwrites: if one screen holds old label-time values while another changes them, saving doneness could restore the old values. That matters in collaborative or multi-tab systems, but much less in this private single-user flow.

Spot patches avoid overwriting unrelated fields and make doneness enrichment small. However, they introduce three states for nullable fields:

- Property omitted: leave unchanged.
- `doneness: null`: clear it.
- `doneness: "dark"`: set it.

They also allow more partial-state combinations that the server must validate.

A better fit here may be explicit operations:

- `createSighting(...)`
- `updateSighting(...)` for the full correction form
- `setSightingDoneness(id, doneness | null)` for post-save enrichment

That avoids generic patch ambiguity and prevents enrichment from touching label time. I recommend these explicit operations. Does that sound right?
Yeah

Locked in: use explicit `createSighting`, full `updateSighting`, and targeted `setSightingDoneness` operations.

Next: deletion semantics.

I recommend permanent hard deletion by ID, returning the deleted ID or a not-found result. There is no moderation, recovery, synchronization, or audit requirement that justifies a `deleted_at` column and the query complexity of soft deletion. The UI’s explicit confirmation is the safeguard.

Do you agree with hard deletion and no in-app undo/recovery contract?
Yeah

Locked in: deletion is permanent, with no soft-delete or recovery fields.

Next: migration boundary.

The map explicitly permits discarding the existing schema and migrations, and the old database represents the superseded multi-user/location product. I recommend a clean reset:

- Replace the existing schema with the single minimal sightings table.
- Delete the old generated migrations and create one fresh baseline migration.
- Provide no transformation or compatibility path for old data.
- Require deployment against a fresh operator-provided database; existing databases must be recreated explicitly.

This keeps obsolete users, stores, moderation, and authentication concepts from leaking into the new model. Do you agree that preserving existing schema or data is out of scope?
Yup just nuke the old data entirely

Locked in: implementation may destroy the old schema, migrations, and data and start from a fresh database. This decision does not itself delete anything; it authorizes the later implementation boundary.

Next: where should Visit planner analysis live?

I recommend the persistence layer return distinct `(labelDate, labelMinute)` evidence for the requested weekday. Application logic then calculates rolling ±10-minute windows, supporting-date counts, and the relative three-band result.

That keeps the database contract small and testable, naturally exposes the evidence the UI needs, and avoids burying product semantics in elaborate SQL. The expected personal dataset is far too small for this in-memory calculation to be concerning.

The alternative is having PostgreSQL calculate the final planner band and count, which reduces transferred rows but tightly couples evolving product rules to a complex query.

Do you agree that persistence should supply weekday evidence while application logic performs the planner analysis?
we can pencil in app logic for analysis, but with a plan to fallback to postgres to do the calculations if it ends up being too slow

Locked in: planner analysis starts in application logic, using distinct weekday evidence from persistence. If profiling shows it is too slow, the calculation may move into PostgreSQL without changing its observable result.

Next: indexes.

I recommend only:

- The automatic primary-key index on `id`.
- A descending index on `(created_at, id)` for deterministic Recent Sightings retrieval.

I would not add a planner index initially. Extracting a weekday from `label_date` may prevent an ordinary date index from helping, while the private dataset should remain small. If profiling motivates PostgreSQL-side analysis, add an expression or generated-weekday index based on the final query.

Do you agree with those two initial indexes and evidence-driven planner indexing later?
yup

Locked in: primary-key and Recent Sightings indexes only; planner indexing waits for measured need.

Next: how should `updated_at` be maintained?

I recommend the application set `updated_at = now()` in every update operation, while PostgreSQL supplies `DEFAULT now()` for both timestamps on creation. A database trigger would protect against forgotten updates from ad hoc SQL, but it adds a function and trigger to an otherwise tiny schema.

Because all supported writes go through the three explicit application operations, the simpler application-managed approach is sufficient and testable.

Do you agree, or would you prefer the database-enforced trigger?
thats fine

Locked in: PostgreSQL defaults both audit timestamps; supported application updates advance `updated_at` explicitly.

The final remaining decision is the read contract. I recommend exactly three persistence queries:

- `getSighting(id)` for correction, returning one sighting or not found.
- `listRecentSightings(limit)` ordered by `created_at DESC, id DESC`; the Capture screen requests three.
- `listWeekdayEvidence(weekday)` returning distinct `labelDate` and `labelMinute` pairs for that literal weekday, ordered by date and minute. Application logic derives the planner result.

No general-purpose list/search API is needed yet. The deferred historical grid can add a purpose-built query when implemented.

Do you agree with this minimal read contract?
looks about right

One edge case remains before I can call the contract implementation-ready:

For “Monday around 12:05 AM,” a literal ±10-minute window crosses into Sunday at 11:55 PM. I recommend keeping evidence strictly on the selected weekday and clipping the window at midnight. The planner is explicitly comparing times on the same weekday, and Costco is closed near midnight anyway.

const r = await tools.exec_command({cmd:"gh issue comment 7 --body-file - <<'EOF'
## Resolution

Use one `sightings` table as the complete persistence model for the private core loop.

### Schema contract

- `id integer GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY`: server-generated sighting identity. Duplicate label dates and times are valid; label time is data, not identity.
- `label_date date NOT NULL`: the literal calendar date printed on the label.
- `label_minute smallint NOT NULL CHECK (label_minute BETWEEN 0 AND 1439)`: the printed clock minute represented as minutes after midnight. Formatting such as `2:30 PM` exists only at application boundaries.
- `doneness text NULL CHECK (doneness IN ('light', 'medium', 'dark'))`: `NULL` means no doneness was recorded. Empty or differently-cased strings are invalid.
- `created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()`: the immutable durable-save instant.
- `updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()`: advanced explicitly by every supported application update.

PostgreSQL's `date` type supplies real-calendar-date validation. There is no uniqueness constraint on label facts, no timezone or offset column, no seconds, no location/user ownership, and no soft-delete or concurrency-version field. Outside-store-hours label times remain valid data and produce only the previously resolved non-blocking UI warning.

### Indexes

- The primary key supplies the identity index.
- Add `(created_at DESC, id DESC)` for deterministic Recent Sightings retrieval.
- Add no planner-specific index initially. Introduce an expression/generated-weekday index only if profiling a later PostgreSQL-side planner query shows a need.

### Mutation contract

- `createSighting`: accepts required label date and minute plus optional doneness, durably inserts, and returns the complete sighting. Save-then-enrich may create with `NULL` doneness.
- `updateSighting`: full replacement of label date, label minute, and nullable doneness for the correction flow; advances `updated_at` and returns the complete sighting.
- `setSightingDoneness`: targeted enrichment or clearing by identity; changes no label facts, advances `updated_at`, and returns the complete sighting.
- `deleteSighting`: permanently deletes by identity after the UI's explicit confirmation and returns the deleted identity or a structured not-found result. There is no in-app recovery contract.

Supported writes use these explicit operations rather than a generic patch. No optimistic locking is required for the one-person, one-expected-writer application.

### Read and analysis contract

- `getSighting(id)` returns the sighting or a structured not-found result for correction.
- `listRecentSightings(limit)` orders by `created_at DESC, id DESC`; Capture requests three. Backfilled or edited label time does not control recency, and editing does not move an old sighting to the top.
- `listWeekdayEvidence(weekday)` returns distinct `(label_date, label_minute)` pairs for the requested literal weekday in deterministic date/minute order.

The application initially calculates rolling ±10-minute matches, distinct supporting-date counts, and relative planner bands from weekday evidence. Windows stay within the selected weekday; they do not cross midnight. If measured performance becomes inadequate, the same observable analysis may move into PostgreSQL and gain a query-specific index.

No general search/list contract is required. The deferred historical grid receives its own purpose-built query when implemented.

### Reset boundary

Delete the superseded schema and generated migrations, create one fresh baseline migration, and preserve no existing data or compatibility path. Deployment requires a fresh operator-provided database; recreation of an old database is explicit and destructive.

### Rationale

Separate `date` and numeric minute fields preserve the timezone-free printed facts and keep sorting, windowing, and bucketing straightforward. Constrained text keeps doneness readable without a PostgreSQL enum or numeric code map. The small explicit operation/query surface supports the resolved Capture and Visit planner behavior while postponing speculative analysis machinery.
EOF
